newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court denies Kevorkian injunction appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court denies Kevorkian injunction appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court Tuesday denied an appeal by retired pathologist Jack Kevorkian over a 1991 injunction that barred him from using his home-built "suicide machine" on terminally ill patients.
Kevorkian, 68, the nation's best known advocate of assisted suicide who has publicly acknowledged attending more than 40 deaths since 1990, had appealed to the high court to hear his case.

But the justices, without comment or dissent, let stand a Michigan Supreme Court ruling in April that upheld the injunction barring him from using the suicide machine, other devices or drugs to hasten a person's death.

Since 1995, Kevorkian twice has been acquitted of assisted suicide charges. He has continued to assist people who want to commit suicide, most recently last week when he helped a 69-year-old man suffering from multiple sclerosis.
He designed the lethal injection machine and used it on his first patient in 1990, prompting the injunction. Most of his patients since have died by inhaling carbon monoxide gas.

The high court's action marked the second time it has rejected a Kevorkian appeal. In 1995 it turned down his appeal of a state high court decision that there is no constitutional right to assisted suicide.

But the Supreme Court this month announced it would enter the right-to-die controversy and decide whether mentally compentent, terminally ill patients may seek help from their doctors in committing suicide. They will hear arguments early next year in cases from New York and Washington on whether states may ban doctor-assisted suicide.

Kevorkian in his appeal charged that the injunction, which prohibits the offering or conducting of any acts to help a patient to commit suicide, impermissibly burdens First Amendment rights. He also argued that mentally competent, terminally ill adults have the right to end their suffering and pain by choosing to hasten their death.
